sentences.text: This extinct bird possessed a rounded head roughly 31.8 mm long, where the beak made up approximately half the total length.
The beak was straight and pointed, featuring an elongated nostril opening.
This specific beak shape implies the rostrum might have moved in a unique way known as rhynchokinetism.
The eye socket was roughly equal in size to the skull base, surrounded by a ring of twelve bone segments.
Its spine contained twenty-one vertebrae before the tail, each showing a hollowed condition called pleurocoelous.
The lower leg bone resembles that of Pumiliornis and includes a special joint surface suggesting at least semi-zygodactyly.
A long hallux with a large, curved claw indicates toe proportions unsuited for walking on the ground.
The second toe had restricted side-to-side movement, likely an adaptation for climbing surfaces.
Fish bones were preserved inside the body of the main specimen, alongside other fish fossils found nearby.
This species lived during the Ypresian stage, between 56 and 48.07 million years ago.
The primary specimen was gathered from the base of a cliff in the northwestern corner of the island of Mors.
The genus name combines the island name Mors with Latin words for shore and bird.
The species name sedilis refers to the ability to perch, derived from Latin terms meaning to sit still.
Mayr established the new family Morsoravidae in 2023, using Morsoravis as the type genus and including Pumiliornis and Sororavis.
Morsoravis was an extinct neoavian bird that inhabited Denmark during the Early Eocene.
Remains of this bird have also been discovered in the Green River Formation of Wyoming and possibly the Nanjemoy Formation of Virginia.
